newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN doubtful on Serb enclave elections in December.
newsitem.headline: UN doubtful on Serb enclave elections in December.

text.p: A senior United Nations official said on Thursday Croatia's demand for early elections in a rebel Serb enclave due to return to Zagreb's control probably cannot be met.

The Zagreb government has called for elections in Eastern Slavonia on December 15 -- a month before the expiry of the U.N.'s administrative mandate there -- in a bid to thwart a Serb campaign for an extension of U.N. control.

"Fundamentally, we don't think conditions can be met for free and fair elections by December 15," Derek Boothby, deputy administrator in the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia, told Reuters by telephone from Vukovar.

"But we are not hanging around deliberately slow-rolling things," he said in response to Croat allegations that UNTAES was being manipulated by the Serbs into prolonging and watering down a "reintegration" process.
"We are trying to move seriously and objectively forward so that when the elections are held they can be seen to be free and fair by both sides and the international community."
UNTAES this week named a chief electoral officer to head a joint Croat-Serb commission that will plan elections in the fertile, oil rich region bordering Serbia.
The balloting must be conducted at least 30 days before UNTAES' mandate ends.

But the date of expiry has yet to be decided by the U.N. Security Council. And staging elections in the wake of wartime upheaval, with two factions disputing conditions including population figures, will be no easy feat.
Croatian leaders and UNTAES administrator Jacques Klein, a U.S. diplomat, agreed on Tuesday that Croatian authority should be reinstated in Eastern Slavonia by spring 1997.
Some 5,000 U.N. troops who have been securing the enclave since January would withdraw by early summer under this plan.

The Serbs' request for a one-year extension of UNTAES, to January 15, 1998, will be weighed by the Security Council. But it will probably rule -- by December -- for an earlier handover in keeping with Klein's recommendation.
That does not mean elections would be feasible in December, Boothby emphasised.
He said the electoral committee had to resolve complicated, politically charged issues such as who would be eligible to vote as well as whom and what citizens would vote for.

Croatia says voting must be limited to people who lived in Eastern Slavonia in 1991, the year minority Serbs seized parts of Croatia in a war against its move to independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia.
Croats were the largest single community in Eastern Slavonia -- closely followed by Serbs -- before 80,000 fled or were driven out by Serb forces in the war.

The area's current population of roughly 130,000, by U.N. estimate, is overwhelmingly Serb, at least 25 percent of them refugees from former separatist pockets that fell to government offensives in 1995.
Croat refugees will return to Eastern Slavonia in the U.N.-run transition period but Serb authorities still hope to assert majority autonomy by having post-1991 Serb settlers vote.

Zagreb says this group must vacate the region to make way for Croats. But Serb refugees fear persecution if they returned to western Croatia and could count on little more than squalid camps and resentment if they went to impoverished Serbia.
